Formula Interface of the Estimation and Testing Functions

Source: R/formula_interface.R
formula_interface.Rd

The estimation and testing functions and kmcurve_fast take vectors of times, event indicators, and group labels, which suits repeated calls inside a simulation loop. For the analysis of a single data set they also accept a model formula with a Surv(time, event) response and a data frame, as the functions of the survival package do:


coxph_fast(Surv(time, status) ~ arm, data = d)
survdiff_fast(Surv(time, status) ~ arm + strata(region), data = d)
rmst_fast(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = d, tau = 12)

The formula is given as the first argument (by position, or by the name of that argument, such as time; there is no argument named formula), and the data frame as data or as the second argument. The other arguments (side, tau, conf.level, and so on) are given by name as with the vector interface, and the result is the same as that of the vector interface with the vectors evaluated from the formula.

Details

The response must be Surv(time, event) with right-censored data, where event is 1 (or TRUE) for an event and 0 (or FALSE) for a censored time; an expression such as Surv(time, status == 2) may be used. A status coded 1 (censored) and 2 (event), as in data sets of the survival package, gives an error that suggests this expression. The call to Surv() is read from the formula and not evaluated, so the survival package need not be attached. Other forms of Surv(), such as counting-process data, are not supported.

The right-hand side is 1 for a single group, or a single group variable with exactly two distinct values for a two-group comparison. Which of the two is allowed follows the vector interface of each function: survfit_fast takes only ~ 1; rmst_fast, wmst_fast, medsurv_fast, and kmcurve_fast take ~ 1 or a group variable; the other functions require a group variable. survdiff_fast and coxph_fast also accept strata() terms, such as arm + strata(region) or arm + strata(region, sex); several stratification variables define a stratum for each combination of their values. Interactions, further covariates, and other formula operators are not supported, because the functions compare two groups without adjustment.

With a group variable, control defaults to its first level: the first level of a factor that occurs in the data, and otherwise the smallest value. This is the reference level of a model formula with the group variable as a factor. control can be given to choose the other group as the control group. A numeric group variable is treated as two groups, whereas survival::coxph() treats it as a continuous covariate, so the coefficient of survival::coxph() equals the log hazard ratio of the two groups only when the two values differ by 1.

The variables are evaluated in data, and variables not found there in the environment of the formula. Missing values in the variables of the formula are an error, as in the vector interface; remove the incomplete rows first, for example with na.omit().

The formula interface adds the cost of evaluating the formula to every call, so the vector interface, with presorted = TRUE where available, remains the choice inside simulation loops.

See also

as.data.frame.fastsurv for the results as data frames.

Examples

library(survival)

# The same hazard ratio from the formula and from the vectors
coxph_fast(Surv(futime, fustat) ~ rx, data = ovarian)
#> Pike-Halley estimator for the hazard ratio (two-group)
#> 
#>   control = 1
#>   alternative = two.sided
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>          coef exp(coef) se(coef)      z Pr(>|z|)
#> group -0.5964    0.5508   0.5868 -1.016     0.31
#> 
#> Hazard ratio and 95% Wald confidence interval:
#>       exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
#> group    0.5508     1.8155    0.1744    1.7399
coxph_fast(ovarian$futime, ovarian$fustat, ovarian$rx, control = 1)
#> Pike-Halley estimator for the hazard ratio (two-group)
#> 
#>   control = 1
#>   alternative = two.sided
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>          coef exp(coef) se(coef)      z Pr(>|z|)
#> group -0.5964    0.5508   0.5868 -1.016     0.31
#> 
#> Hazard ratio and 95% Wald confidence interval:
#>       exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
#> group    0.5508     1.8155    0.1744    1.7399

# Stratified log-rank test
survdiff_fast(Surv(futime, fustat) ~ rx + strata(resid.ds), data = ovarian)
#> Stratified log-rank test (two-group, 2 strata)
#> 
#>   N = 26,  control = 1
#> 
#>           Observed Expected (O-E)^2/E (O-E)^2/V
#> control          7   5.0952    0.7121    1.2796
#> treatment        5   6.9048    0.5255    1.2796
#> 
#>  Chi-square = 1.28 on 1 df,  p-value = 0.258  
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

# Single-group and two-group restricted mean survival time
rmst_fast(Surv(futime, fustat) ~ 1, data = ovarian, tau = 600)
#> Restricted mean survival time (single-group)
#> 
#>   tau = 600
#> 
#>               RMST std.err lower 95% upper 95%
#> tau = 600 480.6607 33.0567  415.8707  545.4507
rmst_fast(Surv(futime, fustat) ~ rx, data = ovarian, tau = 600, control = 2)
#> Restricted mean survival time (two-group)
#> 
#>   tau = 600,  control = 2
#>   alternative = two.sided
#> 
#>               RMST
#> control   534.9060
#> treatment 427.5385
#> 
#>                                       Est. lower 95% upper 95%      z Pr(>|z|)
#> difference (treatment - control) -107.3675 -230.0450   15.3100 -1.715   0.0863
#> ratio (treatment / control)         0.7993    0.6052    1.0555 -1.579   0.1143
#>                                   
#> difference (treatment - control) .
#> ratio (treatment / control)       
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
